items.stem: An atom has 13 protons and 14 neutrons. Which element is it?
items.answer: Aluminium
items.markingKey: A. The number of protons (atomic number 13) identifies aluminium.

items.stem: Explain why the atomic number, not the mass number, identifies an element.
items.answer: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; the number of neutrons (and so mass number) can vary between isotopes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; the number of neutrons (and so mass number) can vary between isotopes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Tariq writes: "A chloride ion, Cl⁻, has one more proton than a chlorine atom." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions.
items.markingKey: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that electrons orbit inside the nucleus. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Electrons are found in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus; the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Electrons are found in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus; the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Priya used a Geiger counter (with the background count subtracted) to measure the count rate from a beta source (beta particles are high-speed electrons emitted from the nucleus) through different thicknesses of aluminium.

Aluminium thickness / mm | Count rate / counts per minute: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.0 | 808 | 786 | 793
0.5 | 410 | 392 | 383
1.0 | 191 | 201 | 193
1.5 | 100 | 101 | 99
2.0 | 49 | 47 | 47

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The count rate decreases as the thickness of aluminium increases, falling by roughly half for each 0.5 mm. Beta particles are electrons that interact with the atoms of aluminium and are gradually absorbed; a few millimetres of aluminium stop almost all of them.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The count rate decreases as the thickness of aluminium increases, falling by roughly half for each 0.5 mm.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Beta particles are electrons that interact with the atoms of aluminium and are gradually absorbed; a few millimetres of aluminium stop almost all of them.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into how the number of protons in a nucleus affects the percentage of alpha particles deflected by more than 30°, using a Rutherford scattering simulation.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how the same simulation settings (atom spacing, view) will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does number of protons in the target nucleus affect percentage of 1000 alpha particles deflected by more than 30°? (b) number of protons in the target nucleus (e.g. 20, 40, 60, 79, 92 in the simulation) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) percentage of 1000 alpha particles deflected by more than 30°, counted by the simulation; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) the same simulation settings (atom spacing, view) – changes the number of close approaches. (e) screen breaks every 20 minutes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why the same simulation settings (atom spacing, view) is controlled (changes the number of close approaches). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. screen breaks every 20 minutes.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that models of the atom used in school are “wrong” and should not be taught.
items.answer: Simplified models are valuable when their limitations are made clear; all scientific models are approximations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the shell model is a simplification; electrons are actually described by orbitals; simple models can create misconceptions. Arguments against: models are useful if they explain observations at the right level; the shell model explains bonding, groups and reactivity well; science progresses by refining models. Supported judgement: Simplified models are valuable when their limitations are made clear; all scientific models are approximations.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the number of protons in a nucleus affects the percentage of alpha particles deflected by more than 30°, using a Rutherford scattering simulation. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): screen breaks every 20 minutes. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. screen breaks every 20 minutes); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which particle has the smallest mass?
items.answer: Electron
items.markingKey: B. An electron has about 1/1840 of the mass of a proton.

items.stem: Explain why the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
items.answer: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, while electrons have a relative mass of only about 1/1840, so almost all the mass is in the nucleus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of 1, while electrons have a relative mass of only about 1/1840, so almost all the mass is in the nucleus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Deduce the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom of iron-56 (atomic number 26).
items.answer: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons
items.markingKey: 1 protons = atomic number = 26; 1 neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30; 1 electrons = protons = 26 (neutral atom).

items.stem: A particle X has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. (a) Identify X, giving its symbol, mass number and charge. (b) Explain how X was formed from a neutral atom. (c) Explain why X has the same mass number as the atom it was formed from.
items.answer: (a) Cl−, mass number 35 (chlorine ion) (b) the atom gained 1 electron(s) (c) electrons have negligible mass; protons and neutrons are unchanged
items.markingKey: (a) 1 chlorine because 17 protons; 1 mass number 17 + 18 = 35; 1 charge 17 − 18 = -1. (b) 1 gain of 1 electron(s) to reach a full outer shell. (c) 1 mass number counts only protons and neutrons; electrons have relative mass ≈ 1/1840.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "abundance"?
options: J. J. Thomson’s 1904 model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it
The electrons in the highest occupied shell, which determine an element’s chemical properties
The percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample
The group 17 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules
items.answer: The percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample
items.markingKey: C. "abundance" is the percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample.

items.stem: Explain the difference between relative atomic mass and mass number.
items.answer: Mass number is a whole number for one isotope (protons + neutrons); relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of all the isotopes in a natural sample, often not a whole number.
items.markingKey: Mass number is a whole number for one isotope (protons + neutrons); relative atomic mass is the weighted mean mass of all the isotopes in a natural sample, often not a whole number. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Isotopes of hydrogen have different numbers of protons, which is why they have different masses." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: All hydrogen isotopes have one proton; they differ in neutrons (0, 1, 2).
items.markingKey: All hydrogen isotopes have one proton; they differ in neutrons (0, 1, 2). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Felix measured the count rate of a sample of the radioisotope protactinium-234 at intervals (background subtracted).

Time / s | Count rate / counts per 10 s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 389 | 362 | 370
60 | 209 | 215 | 213
120 | 112 | 117 | 110
180 | 61 | 61 | 62
240 | 35 | 36 | 36

Calculate the mean count rate when the time was 240 s.
items.answer: 35.7 counts per 10 s
items.markingKey: M1 (35 + 36 + 36) ÷ 3; A1 35.7 counts per 10 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Gallium (atomic number 31) has isotopes of mass number 69 and 71. Compare the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms of the two isotopes.
items.answer: Both have 31 protons and 31 electrons; gallium-69 has 38 neutrons and gallium-71 has 40 neutrons.
items.markingKey: 1 same protons (31); 1 same electrons (31); 1 neutrons 38 vs 40.

items.stem: Kenji investigated how the number of “undecayed” dice changes with each throw, to model the half-life of a radioisotope. The method had this weakness: only 20 dice were used. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use at least 100 dice (or pool class results) because random decay averages out only for large numbers
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use at least 100 dice (or pool class results) because random decay averages out only for large numbers

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "abundance".
items.answer: The percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the percentage of atoms of an element that are a particular isotope in a natural sample. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Relative atomic mass is just the mass number of the most common isotope." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is a weighted mean of all isotopes, so it can differ from any single mass number (e.g. Cl = 35.5).
items.markingKey: It is a weighted mean of all isotopes, so it can differ from any single mass number (e.g. Cl = 35.5). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A natural sample of magnesium contains these isotopes: magnesium-24 (79.0%), magnesium-25 (10.0%), magnesium-26 (11.0%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium to 1 decimal place.

Natural uranium is 0.72% uranium-235 and 99.28% uranium-238. Nuclear fuel is “enriched” to 3.0% uranium-235. (a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of natural and of enriched uranium to 3 decimal places. (b) Explain why the isotopes cannot be separated by a chemical reaction. (c) Discuss one benefit and one risk of uranium enrichment technology.
items.answer: (a) natural 237.978; enriched 237.910 (b) isotopes have the same electron arrangement, so identical chemical properties (c) benefit: low-carbon electricity; risk: highly enriched uranium can be used in nuclear weapons
items.markingKey: (a) M1 weighted mean; A1 237.978; A1 237.910. (b) 1 same number of electrons → same chemistry; separation uses mass difference (centrifuges). (c) 1 benefit, 1 risk with explanation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "electron shell (energy level)".
items.answer: A region around the nucleus where electrons with a particular energy are found
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a region around the nucleus where electrons with a particular energy are found. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a group and a period.
items.answer: A group is a vertical column of elements with the same number of outer electrons; a period is a horizontal row of elements with the same number of occupied shells.
items.markingKey: A group is a vertical column of elements with the same number of outer electrons; a period is a horizontal row of elements with the same number of occupied shells. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that potassium has the electron arrangement 2,8,9. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The third shell holds 8 before the fourth starts for the first 20 elements: potassium is 2,8,8,1.
items.markingKey: The third shell holds 8 before the fourth starts for the first 20 elements: potassium is 2,8,8,1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that elements in the same period have similar properties because they have the same number of shells. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Properties change across a period; similar properties belong to elements in the same group.
items.markingKey: Properties change across a period; similar properties belong to elements in the same group. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lukas is investigating how the metal ion in a compound affects the colour of light emitted in a flame test, measured with a spectroscope. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: metal ion in the chloride (lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, copper)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal ion in the chloride (lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, copper) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Aiko compared published values (from three data books) of the atomic radius of group 1 elements.

Number of occupied shells | Atomic radius / pm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 172 | 165 | 174
3 | 204 | 215 | 200
4 | 255 | 262 | 260
5 | 273 | 277 | 280

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: Atomic radius increases as the number of occupied electron shells increases. Each extra shell places the outer electron further from the nucleus; inner shells shield it, which is also why reactivity increases down group 1.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: Atomic radius increases as the number of occupied electron shells increases.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Each extra shell places the outer electron further from the nucleus; inner shells shield it, which is also why reactivity increases down group 1.

items.stem: Mohammed investigated how the metal ion in a compound affects the colour of light emitted in a flame test, measured with a spectroscope. The method had this weakness: the same loop was used without cleaning between samples. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: clean the loop in acid and flame it until no colour appears before each test
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: clean the loop in acid and flame it until no colour appears before each test

items.stem: "The shell model of electron arrangement is a good enough model for MYP chemistry." Discuss.
items.answer: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains groups, periods, ion charges and bonding; simple to draw and use. Arguments against: does not explain elements beyond calcium (transition metals) well; electrons are not in fixed circular orbits; quantum model uses orbitals. Supported judgement: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Briefly explain why elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.
items.answer: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and reactions involve outer electrons being lost, gained or shared.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and reactions involve outer electrons being lost, gained or shared. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana writes: "Potassium has the electron arrangement 2,8,9." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The third shell holds 8 before the fourth starts for the first 20 elements: potassium is 2,8,8,1.
items.markingKey: The third shell holds 8 before the fourth starts for the first 20 elements: potassium is 2,8,8,1. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe neon advertising signs and explain what it reveals about electron energy levels.
items.answer: Electricity passed through neon gas excites electrons, which then fall back to lower shells, emitting red-orange light. The colour depends on the energy gaps between neon’s shells.
items.markingKey: Context (Electricity passed through neon gas excites electrons, which then fall back to lower shells, emitting red-orange light.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The colour depends on the energy gaps between neon’s shells. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electron energy levels.

items.stem: Element X has atomic number 12 and element Y has atomic number 7. (a) Write the electron arrangement of each atom. (b) Predict the charge on the ion each forms and explain your prediction. (c) Deduce the formula of the compound formed between X and Y.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 each arrangement. (b) 1 X loses 2 outer electron(s) → +2; 1 Y gains 3 → −3; full outer shells. (c) M1 charges balance: 3 × 2 = 2 × 3; A1 X3Y2.

items.stem: Which gas is produced when sodium reacts with water?
items.answer: Hydrogen
items.markingKey: A. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂

items.stem: Maya writes: "Sodium is a hard, dense metal that sinks in water." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sodium is soft (cut with a knife) and less dense than water, so it floats and fizzes.
items.markingKey: Sodium is soft (cut with a knife) and less dense than water, so it floats and fizzes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Group 1 metals become less reactive down the group because they get heavier." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
items.markingKey: Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Omar adds iodine water to potassium chloride solution. Predict whether a reaction occurs. If it does, write the word and balanced symbol equations and describe what is seen.
items.answer: No reaction: iodine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace it.
items.markingKey: 1 no reaction; 1 reason: iodine is below chlorine in group 17 (less reactive); 1 no colour change beyond that of the halogen water.

items.stem: Tariq is investigating how the position of a halogen in group 17 affects whether it can displace other halogens from their salt solutions. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: the halogen solution added (chlorine water, bromine water, iodine solution)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the halogen solution added (chlorine water, bromine water, iodine solution) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The growing demand for lithium for batteries is good for the environment."
items.answer: Lithium enables a low-carbon transition, but mining must be managed responsibly and recycling increased.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electric vehicles reduce CO₂ emissions and urban air pollution; batteries store renewable energy. Arguments against: lithium mining in the Atacama uses huge volumes of water in a desert; impacts on local and Indigenous communities; battery recycling is limited. Supported judgement: Lithium enables a low-carbon transition, but mining must be managed responsibly and recycling increased.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "halogens".
items.answer: The group 17 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the group 17 elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine): reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between trends in reactivity in group 17 and trends in reactivity in group 1.
items.answer: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group (electron lost more easily); group 17 reactivity decreases down the group (electron gained less easily).
items.markingKey: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group (electron lost more easily); group 17 reactivity decreases down the group (electron gained less easily). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to lithium-ion batteries, explain how it illustrates group 1 properties.
items.answer: Phones and electric cars use lithium, the lightest metal, because it gives up its outer electron readily and stores a lot of energy per kilogram. Lithium’s single outer electron is easily lost, making it a good material for storing charge.
items.markingKey: Context (Phones and electric cars use lithium, the lightest metal, because it gives up its outer electron readily and stores a lot of energy per kilogram.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lithium’s single outer electron is easily lost, making it a good material for storing charge. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to group 1 properties.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Rutherford’s 1911 model of the atom with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus surrounded mostly by empty space containing electrons"?
items.answer: nuclear model
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of nuclear model.

items.stem: "Most alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most passed straight through, showing the atom is mostly empty space; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected back.
items.markingKey: Most passed straight through, showing the atom is mostly empty space; only about 1 in 8000 was deflected back. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Geiger and Marsden’s gold foil experiment (Manchester, 1909) and explain what it reveals about the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back. Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: Context (Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the nuclear model of the atom.

items.stem: With reference to Geiger and Marsden’s gold foil experiment (Manchester, 1909), explain how it illustrates the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back. Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: Context (Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the nuclear model of the atom.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Mendeleev deserves most of the credit for the periodic table.
items.answer: Mendeleev’s predictions make his contribution the most important, but the table is the work of many scientists.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: he left gaps and made accurate predictions that were later confirmed; he swapped elements (e.g. Te and I) to match properties. Arguments against: Newlands (law of octaves, 1865) and Meyer had similar ideas; Moseley’s work on atomic number fixed the ordering problems; Ramsay added the noble gases. Supported judgement: Mendeleev’s predictions make his contribution the most important, but the table is the work of many scientists.

items.stem: Explain why Rutherford’s gold foil results could not be explained by the plum pudding model.
items.answer: In the plum pudding model positive charge is spread out, so alpha particles would pass through with tiny deflections; some were deflected by large angles or bounced back, which needs a small, concentrated positive nucleus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the plum pudding model positive charge is spread out, so alpha particles would pass through with tiny deflections; some were deflected by large angles or bounced back, which needs a small, concentrated positive nucleus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

“It was quite the most incredible event that has ever happened to me in my life. It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.”
— Ernest Rutherford, describing the gold foil results

Explain what Rutherford meant and what conclusion he drew about the structure of the atom.
items.answer: He was surprised that heavy, fast alpha particles bounced back from very thin foil; this was impossible if positive charge was spread out (plum pudding), so he concluded that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
items.markingKey: He was surprised that heavy, fast alpha particles bounced back from very thin foil; this was impossible if positive charge was spread out (plum pudding), so he concluded that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nucleus"?
options: A region around the nucleus where electrons with a particular energy are found
An arrangement of the elements in order of increasing atomic number, in groups and periods, so that elements with similar properties line up
The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electrical charge
items.answer: The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons
items.markingKey: C. "nucleus" is the tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.

items.stem: Define the term "outer shell (valence) electrons".
items.answer: The electrons in the highest occupied shell, which determine an element’s chemical properties
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the electrons in the highest occupied shell, which determine an element’s chemical properties. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom"?
items.answer: relative atomic mass (Aᵣ)
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of relative atomic mass (Aᵣ).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the melting point of the halogens increases down the group.
items.answer: The molecules get larger with more electrons, so the intermolecular forces between molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The molecules get larger with more electrons, so the intermolecular forces between molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Mendeleev’s table was accepted immediately because it was complete." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It became widely accepted after his predicted elements (gallium 1875, germanium 1886) were discovered with properties close to his predictions.
items.markingKey: It became widely accepted after his predicted elements (gallium 1875, germanium 1886) were discovered with properties close to his predictions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between atomic number and mass number.
items.answer: Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons + neutrons.
items.markingKey: Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons + neutrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why noble gases are unreactive.
items.answer: They have a full outer shell of electrons (2 for helium, 8 for the others), which is very stable, so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have a full outer shell of electrons (2 for helium, 8 for the others), which is very stable, so they do not need to lose, gain or share electrons. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why isotopes of an element can have different physical properties, such as density.
items.answer: They have different numbers of neutrons, so different masses; e.g. heavy water (D₂O) is about 11% denser than H₂O.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have different numbers of neutrons, so different masses; e.g. heavy water (D₂O) is about 11% denser than H₂O. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why group 1 metals are stored under oil.
items.answer: They react rapidly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; oil keeps air and moisture away.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They react rapidly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; oil keeps air and moisture away. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
In a simulation of the Geiger–Marsden gold foil experiment, Ana counted the alpha particles detected per minute at different scattering angles.

Scattering angle / ° | Alpha particles detected / per minute: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
15 | 4891 | 4774 | 4768
30 | 295 | 317 | 295
45 | 63 | 66 | 65
60 | 22 | 22 | 22
90 | 5 | 5 | 6

State the scattering angle at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 15 °; range = 123 per minute; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 15 °; 1 range = max − min = 4891 − 4768 = 123 per minute; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: A student claims that a chloride ion, Cl⁻, has one more proton than a chlorine atom. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions.
items.markingKey: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using neon advertising signs as an example, explain electron energy levels.
items.answer: Electricity passed through neon gas excites electrons, which then fall back to lower shells, emitting red-orange light. The colour depends on the energy gaps between neon’s shells.
items.markingKey: Context (Electricity passed through neon gas excites electrons, which then fall back to lower shells, emitting red-orange light.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The colour depends on the energy gaps between neon’s shells. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electron energy levels.

items.stem: Briefly describe iodine-131 treatment of overactive thyroid glands and explain what it reveals about isotopes having the same chemical properties.
items.answer: Patients swallow a capsule of radioactive iodine, which the thyroid absorbs because it uses iodine to make thyroxine. The body treats I-131 exactly like stable iodine, so it is taken up by the thyroid, where its radiation destroys overactive tissue.
items.markingKey: Context (Patients swallow a capsule of radioactive iodine, which the thyroid absorbs because it uses iodine to make thyroxine.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The body treats I-131 exactly like stable iodine, so it is taken up by the thyroid, where its radiation destroys overactive tissue. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to isotopes having the same chemical properties.

items.stem: Using lithium-ion batteries as an example, explain group 1 properties.
items.answer: Phones and electric cars use lithium, the lightest metal, because it gives up its outer electron readily and stores a lot of energy per kilogram. Lithium’s single outer electron is easily lost, making it a good material for storing charge.
items.markingKey: Context (Phones and electric cars use lithium, the lightest metal, because it gives up its outer electron readily and stores a lot of energy per kilogram.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lithium’s single outer electron is easily lost, making it a good material for storing charge. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to group 1 properties.

items.stem: Using Geiger and Marsden’s gold foil experiment (Manchester, 1909) as an example, explain the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back. Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.
items.markingKey: Context (Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil mostly passed through, a few were deflected at large angles and some bounced back.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Rutherford concluded the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the nuclear model of the atom.

items.stem: "Electrons orbit inside the nucleus." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Electrons are found in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus; the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons.
items.markingKey: Electrons are found in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus; the nucleus contains only protons and neutrons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the shell model of electron arrangement is a good enough model for MYP chemistry.
items.answer: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains groups, periods, ion charges and bonding; simple to draw and use. Arguments against: does not explain elements beyond calcium (transition metals) well; electrons are not in fixed circular orbits; quantum model uses orbitals. Supported judgement: It is good enough for the first 20 elements and bonding at this level, as long as its limits are recognised.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the medical benefits of radioisotopes outweigh the risks?
items.answer: With careful dosing and short half-lives, benefits usually outweigh risks for patients, but exposure must be minimised for staff and the public.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diagnosis (technetium-99m scans) and cancer treatment save many lives; short half-life isotopes limit exposure. Arguments against: radiation can damage healthy cells and cause cancer; radioactive waste must be stored safely; cost and access issues. Supported judgement: With careful dosing and short half-lives, benefits usually outweigh risks for patients, but exposure must be minimised for staff and the public. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that adding fluoride to public drinking water is a good idea.
items.answer: It is effective at low concentrations; whether it is justified depends on balancing public health against individual choice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reduces tooth decay, especially in children from poorer families; cheap and reaches everyone. Arguments against: people cannot choose whether to take it; too much causes fluorosis; toothpaste already provides fluoride. Supported judgement: It is effective at low concentrations; whether it is justified depends on balancing public health against individual choice. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the thickness of the foil affects the number of alpha particles scattered through large angles, using a gold foil experiment simulation. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): screen breaks every 20 minutes. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. screen breaks every 20 minutes); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electrical charge"?
items.answer: ion
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of ion.

items.stem: Which is the electron arrangement of an atom of sodium (atomic number 11)?
Which statement about isotopes of an element is correct?
options: They have different numbers of electrons in neutral atoms
They have the same chemical properties
They have the same mass number
They have different numbers of protons
items.answer: They have the same chemical properties
items.markingKey: B. Chemistry depends on electrons, which are the same.

items.stem: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
items.answer: Potassium’s outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus with more shielding by inner shells, so the attraction is weaker and it is lost more easily.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Potassium’s outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus with more shielding by inner shells, so the attraction is weaker and it is lost more easily. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Mendeleev’s table was accepted immediately because it was complete." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It became widely accepted after his predicted elements (gallium 1875, germanium 1886) were discovered with properties close to his predictions.
items.markingKey: It became widely accepted after his predicted elements (gallium 1875, germanium 1886) were discovered with properties close to his predictions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mass number and atomic number.
items.answer: Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons + neutrons.
items.markingKey: Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons + neutrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Elements in the same period have similar properties because they have the same number of shells." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Properties change across a period; similar properties belong to elements in the same group.
items.markingKey: Properties change across a period; similar properties belong to elements in the same group. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that isotopes of hydrogen have different numbers of protons, which is why they have different masses. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All hydrogen isotopes have one proton; they differ in neutrons (0, 1, 2).
items.markingKey: All hydrogen isotopes have one proton; they differ in neutrons (0, 1, 2). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Sodium is a hard, dense metal that sinks in water." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Sodium is soft (cut with a knife) and less dense than water, so it floats and fizzes.
items.markingKey: Sodium is soft (cut with a knife) and less dense than water, so it floats and fizzes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the thickness of the foil affects the number of alpha particles scattered through large angles, using a gold foil experiment simulation, explain why the same target element (gold) must be kept the same in every trial.
items.answer: nuclear charge affects scattering
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the same target element (gold) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: nuclear charge affects scattering. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: "A chloride ion, Cl⁻, has one more proton than a chlorine atom." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions.
items.markingKey: It has one more electron; the number of protons (17) never changes in chemical reactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Niels Bohr’s explanation of hydrogen’s line spectrum (1913) as an example, explain electrons in shells (energy levels).
items.answer: Hydrogen gas emits only certain colours of light; Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed energy levels and emit light when they drop between them. Only specific energy differences are possible, so only specific wavelengths of light are emitted – evidence for shells.
items.markingKey: Context (Hydrogen gas emits only certain colours of light; Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed energy levels and emit light when they drop between them.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Only specific energy differences are possible, so only specific wavelengths of light are emitted – evidence for shells. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electrons in shells (energy levels).

items.stem: A student claims that the mass number of an atom is the number of protons plus electrons. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mass number is protons plus neutrons; electrons have negligible mass.

items.stem: Element X has atomic number 11 and element Y has atomic number 8. (a) Write the electron arrangement of each atom. (b) Predict the charge on the ion each forms and explain your prediction. (c) Deduce the formula of the compound formed between X and Y.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 each arrangement. (b) 1 X loses 1 outer electron(s) → +1; 1 Y gains 2 → −2; full outer shells. (c) M1 charges balance: 2 × 1 = 1 × 2; A1 X2Y.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the growing demand for lithium for batteries is good for the environment?
items.answer: Lithium enables a low-carbon transition, but mining must be managed responsibly and recycling increased.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electric vehicles reduce CO₂ emissions and urban air pollution; batteries store renewable energy. Arguments against: lithium mining in the Atacama uses huge volumes of water in a desert; impacts on local and Indigenous communities; battery recycling is limited. items.stem: Mendeleev predicted that eka-aluminium would have a relative atomic mass of about 68, a density of about 5.9 g/cm³ and a low melting point. Gallium, discovered in 1875, has Aᵣ 69.7, density 5.91 g/cm³ and melts at 30 °C. Evaluate how well this supports Mendeleev’s periodic table and explain why scientists value successful predictions.
items.answer: Very close agreement (mass within 3%, density almost exact, low melting point correct) strongly supports the periodic table, because Mendeleev made the prediction before the element was known; a model that predicts new results is more convincing than one that only fits known data.
items.markingKey: Very close agreement (mass within 3%, density almost exact, low melting point correct) strongly supports the periodic table, because Mendeleev made the prediction before the element was known; a model that predicts new results is more convincing than one that only fits known data.
